title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Tool‑Augmented Agent vs LLM‑Only Generation for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id: cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) to evaluate whether adding a deterministic NetOps verifier and a lightweight topology simulator (a tool‑augmented guarded pipeline) changes deterministic‑validator pass outcomes relative to an LLM‑only baseline when the same single LLM candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned n=300 paired tasks; 299 complete analyzable pairs. Deterministic validator passes: baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299 (contingency n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired difference = 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI [0.00,0.00], 10k resamples, seed=1729). Because the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the experiment answers the narrower question of whether downstream tool/validator processing changes pass/fail for identical LLM candidates; it does not test whether independent agentic tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer candidates. All raw responses, validator traces, provider traces, execution logs, and SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived and cited in the Disclosure; representative artifacts and exact counts are reported in the body.

sections.introduction: Motivation and scope. Translating high‑level operator intent into device configuration is a core NetOps task. Practical automation proposals increasingly pair a generative LLM with deterministic validators, simulators, or repair loops to reduce misconfiguration risk. We preregistered a concrete, artifact‑anchored experimental question within this space: given identical LLM candidate outputs (shared_initial_candidate semantics), does downstream tool‑augmentation (deterministic verifier + lightweight simulator) change deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcomes? This design isolates downstream processing from generation variance and answers an operationally useful, narrowly defined estimand (tool/verifier processing effect on a fixed set of candidates). It does not address independent per‑condition agentic generation; that is left for follow‑up designs. Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired experiment with machine‑readable preregistration (study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) and complete artifact provenance. (2) Exact, reproducible execution accounting and statistical analysis (contingency table, McNemar test, bootstrap CI) derived from archived scoring JSONs and validator traces. (3) A methodological discussion of generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent per‑condition generation), ceiling effects observed in practice, and prescriptive next steps.
sections.related_work: Prior work covers intent→config translation, generate–validate–repair flows, verifier‑assisted agents, and tool‑augmented runtime reliability mechanisms. Representative literature includes intent‑based configuration and LLM translation approaches (Nguyen Tu et al., 2024; PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369), practical RAG/agent tool literature, and verifier‑orchestration analyses. Unlike broad model‑ranking or zero‑shot generator comparisons, our run experimentally isolates downstream validator effects by design and provides full provenance for every reported number.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 was frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on deterministic‑validator pass indicator; primary analysis: exact McNemar two‑sided; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed 1729). Key execution semantics deliberately fixed: shared_initial_candidate — for each paired task, a single LLM generation was produced and reused without modification by both the baseline and the guarded condition. Rationale: isolate downstream verifier/simulator effects. Task bank and strata. 300 paired tasks were sampled from a deterministic synthetic topology pool with explicit intents, initial/final state expectations, dependency/workflow constraints, and difficulty labels (simple vs complex; representative patterns include shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). Inclusion/exclusion and contamination: exact‑string matches to a curated public config corpus were excluded per the preregistration; all detection outputs are logged. Implementation and artifacts. Adapter/orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). All provider calls, raw responses, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and execution logs were recorded; authoritative artifact paths and SHA‑256 hashes are included in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting (authoritative): planned episodes 600 (300 pairs); completed episodes 598; failed episodes 2; complete analyzable pairs 299. Model calls used = 300; maximum_model_calls = 600. Representative artifact locations: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256: 6569b491...); execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha256: cefa6344...); execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha256: b45a6008...). Confirmatory outcome (archival numbers). Contingency (complete pairs n=299): n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Baseline successes = 299/299 (100.0%); guarded successes = 299/299 (100.0%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Missingness and failures. One paired item is missing from the archive (pair‑000269); two failed episodes correspond to that pair (execution/execution_log.jsonl; sha256: b45a60085950...). Deterministic reconciliation. The run's deterministic_reconciliation.json is consistent: completed_episode_count=598; failed_episode_count=2; complete_pair_count=299; provider calls audited (hosted_model_call_event_count=300, completed=299, failed=1). Representative validator traces. Example scoring entries and validator final_state snapshots (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json; execution/scoring/task-000002-*.json; execution/scoring/task-000003-*.json) show parsed_command_count, final_state, difficulty pattern, and validation status; these JSONs are the authoritative evidence for the acceptance decisions and are archived with recorded SHA‑256 hashes.
sections.discussion: Interpretation constrained by generation semantics. The executed estimand asked whether downstream tool‑augmentation changes deterministic‑validator pass outcomes for identical LLM candidates (shared_initial_candidate). On that executed estimand the archived, verifiable result is unequivocal: no change (n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). This outcome is not evidence that permitting the guarded/agentic pipeline to produce independent generations would fail to improve safety: independent per‑condition generation is a different estimand and was not executed here. Ceiling effect and power. The preregistration assumed a baseline pass ≈0.60 and powered n=300 to detect a 0.20 absolute paired difference. The observed baseline success rate = 1.00 (299/299), which violates that assumption and produces a ceiling effect that makes the preregistered minimally important effect unobservable in this run; we therefore treat the original power calculation as inapplicable post hoc and report exact counts and CIs from the observed data. Operational and methodological lessons. (1) Shared_initial_candidate is a defensible design when isolating verifier/tool processing is the scientific goal; it reduces variance from generation but risks ceiling outcomes when candidate quality is high. (2) To evaluate whether agentic tool‑augmented systems improve generation quality, future preregistrations should use independent per‑condition generation semantics, larger/harder task banks to avoid ceiling success rates, and multi‑model replication. (3) Deterministic validators produce rich, auditable traces (parsed_command_count, final_state snapshots, violation codes) that are valuable even when generators already produce high‑quality outputs. Limitations (artifact‑backed). Tasks were synthetic and evaluated with a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor CLIs and production telemetry is limited. Single declared model used (gpt‑5‑mini); multi‑model generality not shown. The validator approximates operational checks but cannot exhaustively emulate all platform heterogeneity. Two technical failures occurred (pair‑000269); logs and provider traces for those failures are archived and referenced above.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics, answers a narrow operational question: given identical LLM candidates, does downstream tool‑augmentation (deterministic verifier + simulator) change deterministic‑validator pass outcomes? For the 299 analyzable paired tasks the answer is no (both conditions accepted the same candidates; n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). This factual result is fully reproducible from the archived artifacts and hashes listed in the execution manifest. It does not address whether agentic tool‑augmented generation (independent per‑condition generation) would produce different or safer outputs; that remains a preregistered follow‑up. We therefore recommend a subsequent confirmatory run with independent per‑condition generation, a harder task pool to avoid ceiling effects, and multi‑model replication. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and execution logs are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement and the execution manifest.

disclosure_statement: This paper and all reported results were produced by an autonomous, post‑lock execution run governed by the frozen master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Preregistration: study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0) was frozen before execution. Declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa) and provider recorded as openai_responses. Orchestration/adapter used: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Generation semantics used in this run: shared_initial_candidate — a single LLM generation was produced and reused across both baseline and guarded conditions; this choice is recorded in the preregistration and the execution manifest and is central to the executed estimand. Tools permitted during execution: deterministic validator and a lightweight topology simulator; the execution contract allowed one repair call per task under the frozen retry policy. Execution accounting (authoritative): planned episodes 600; completed episodes 598; failed episodes 2 (both forming one missing pair, pair-000269). Complete analyzable pairs: 299. Detailed per‑episode failure records, provider error codes, timestamps, and low‑level logs are archived in execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8) and in the provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*; hashes recorded in the execution manifest). All raw model outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, execution logs, and SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived in the execution bundle listed in the execution manifest and are the authoritative source for all numbers reported above. No manual human editing of the manuscript technical content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numeric claims are grounded in the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
limitations: The run used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (single LLM generation reused across both conditions). Consequently, the executed estimand tests whether downstream verifier/tool processing changes pass/fail for identical LLM candidates; it does not test whether independent, agentic tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Tasks were synthetic templates evaluated with a lightweight topology simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, production telemetry, and richer runtime heterogeneity is limited.
Only a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a defined set of dependency/workflow rules (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break); it cannot exhaustively model all platform or hardware idiosyncrasies.

A ceiling effect occurred: the observed baseline success rate (299/299) violated the preregistered power assumption (~0.60), rendering the originally powered contrast (detecting a +0.20 paired difference) uninformative for this execution; this is reported and interpreted transparently.
